questions.q: Who is the poet of "irax", and what is the title of the single long poem (,dek=k laxzg) from which this poem is taken, along with its publication year?
questions.a: The poet is vkyksd èkUok (born 1948, Aligarh). The poem "irax" is an excerpt from his single long poem titled "nqfu;k jks”k curh gS", published in 1998. A wrong answer (e.g., naming a different poet like Kedarnath Singh or misidentifying the source as an early collection like "turk dk vkneh") reveals that the student has not distinguished between the poet's multiple works and the specific magnum opus that defines his late career — a critical error for Board questions on literary history.

questions.q: The NCERT introduction states that the poet never wrote "Fkksd osQ Hkko esa" (in the tone of complaint). Explain in your own words what this means for interpreting "irax", especially given the poem's depiction of vanishing rural landscapes.
questions.a: It means the poet does not use the poem as a platform for explicit protest, polemic, or victimhood; instead, he presents the disappearing world (childhood, nature, rural rhythms) with quiet observational precision, letting the loss speak through imagery rather than argument. A wrong answer that equates "no complaint" with "no criticism" misses the subtlety: the poem *is* a critique of modernity, but enacted through elegy and juxtaposition, not slogan. This distinction is vital for Board "analysis" questions and JEE-style inference traps.

questions.q: The introduction mentions the poet's involvement in "te'ksniqj esa vè;;u&eaMfy;ksa dk lapkyu" (promoting science communication in Tekanpur) and teaching in national institutions. How might this dual identity (poet + science communicator/academic) influence the *precision* and *observational mode* of "irax"? Give one concrete textual expectation.
questions.a: A scientist's trained observation fosters exact, sensory imagery rather than vague sentimentality. Expectation: the poem will use specific, almost cataloguing details of flora, fauna, light, and sound (e.g., names of birds, trees, the quality of dust) — akin to field notes — rather than abstract adjectives like "beautiful" or "sad". A wrong answer that sees no connection between science and poetry overlooks the "nayi kavita" trait of "image as argument" and will struggle with later nodes on imagery (c12_hin_ar_cbse_02_008).

questions.q: Compare the thematic concern of "irax" (as signaled in the intro: "cky fØ;kdykiksa, izo`Qfr esa vk, ifjorZu") with the Class 11 poem "Aroh Chapter 1" (or any Class 11 "Before You Read" you recall). Identify one structural similarity in how *both* NCERT introductions frame the poet's project.
questions.a: Both introductions position the poet as a chronicler of a vanishing world — rural/folk in Class 11 (e.g., Nirala's folk roots or Muktibodh's urban alienation) and childhood/nature here — and both highlight the poet's formal innovation (free verse, long poem, linguistic experimentation) as the *vehicle* for that chronicling, not just decoration. A wrong answer that only lists themes without linking to form misses the Board's emphasis on "form-content unity" and the competitive exam focus on literary history trajectories.

questions.q: The introduction calls "irax" a "yach dfork" (long poem) divided into three parts in the textbook. Evaluate: does this textbook segmentation help or hinder the reader's experience of the original "single long poem" structure? Justify with one argument for each side.
questions.a: Helps: makes a 1998 book-length work accessible in a classroom period, allowing focused study of three distinct tonal phases (childhood idyll, encroaching modernity, elegiac reflection). Hinders: fractures the cumulative, flowing architecture of the "single long poem" where images echo across hundreds of lines; the textbook's "three parts" impose artificial boundaries that may obscure the poem's deliberate refusal of closure. A one-sided answer (only "helps" or only "hinders") shows lack of evaluative nuance required for 6-mark Board questions and CUET critical thinking items.

questions.q: Based *only* on the "Before You Read" context (poet's awards, science background, "no complaint" stance, rural sensibility), write a 4-line stanza in Hindi that *anticipates* the voice and imagery of "irax". Do not copy from the poem.
questions.a:
Example (criteria: uses concrete nature image, no explicit emotion word, precise verb, suggests change):
"बबूल की छाँह में सूखती नदी की रेत,
गिलहरी गिनती है दाने — गिनती ही रह गई।
मास्टर साहब की साइकिल की घंटी अब नहीं बजती,
बस धूल का एक बादल, चुपचाप ठहर गया।"
A poor answer uses abstractions ("बचपन खो गया", "बहुत दुख है") or rhymes forcedly — revealing the student hasn't internalized the "observational precision without complaint" principle.
